questions: Did these abnormal movements begin suddenly?
Do the movements disappear or lessen when you are distracted?
Can you voluntarily stop the movements for a few seconds?
Do the movements occur only when someone is watching or examining you?
Do you experience an irresistible urge before the movements that is relieved afterward?
Have you ever had similar episodes during sleep?
Do you have weakness or numbness on one side of your body?
Have you recently experienced major psychological stress or trauma?
Are the involuntary movements predominantly on the right side of your body?
Do they involve sustained twisting or abnormal postures of the neck, trunk, or limbs?
Do the movements become worse when you try to perform a voluntary action, such as reaching or walking?
Have you noticed progressive changes in memory, judgment, mood, or personality?
Has your speech become slurred or difficult to understand?
Has anyone in your family had similar involuntary movements or an unexplained progressive neurological illness?
Did these movements begin before the age of 50?
Do you take or have you recently taken metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, antipsychotics, or other dopamine-blocking medicines?
Do the abnormal postures cause significant pain or painful muscle cramps?
Do they improve when you touch the affected body part or use another “sensory trick,” such as touching your face or holding a limb?
Did the abnormal postures begin in one limb and gradually spread to other limbs?
Are your arms or hands also affected?
Are your eyes, jaw, tongue, or facial muscles affected by similar involuntary contractions?
Do you have difficulty swallowing or breathing during an episode?
Do the episodes occur continuously while you are awake rather than in brief attacks?
Have you had a previous stroke, head injury, brain infection, or exposure to carbon monoxide or other toxins?
Do the episodes occur suddenly and last from seconds to a few minutes?
Are the episodes triggered by standing, walking, or another sudden voluntary movement?
Are they triggered by startle, emotional excitement, caffeine, alcohol, or prolonged exercise?
Do you remain fully conscious and able to remember the entire episode?
Do you lose consciousness, bite your tongue, or lose bladder control during an episode?
Do the abnormal postures occur on both sides of the body during the same episode?
Do you have symptom-free periods with completely normal movements between episodes?
Have the episodes been increasing in frequency or severity?
Did the dystonia begin in the neck before spreading to the arms and legs?
Is the dystonia worse later in the day and better after sleep?
Have you ever had liver disease, jaundice, unexplained abdominal swelling, or abnormal liver tests?
Have you had psychiatric symptoms such as depression, irritability, or unexplained behavioral changes?
Have you noticed a brown or greenish ring at the edge of your cornea?
Have you ever experienced tremor, slowness, stiffness, or difficulty initiating movement?
Has the dystonia progressively worsened over months or years?
Have you ever had a meaningful improvement after taking levodopa?
orders: Bedside examination for functional movement disorder: assess distractibility, entrainment, variability, and inconsistency of the abnormal postures during contralateral rhythmic tapping and alternative voluntary movements.
Neurological examination for true dystonia, including passive range of motion, strength, reflexes, sensation, coordination, and gait.
MRI of the brain and cervical spine with and without gadolinium.
Serum ceruloplasmin, serum copper, 24-hour urinary copper, liver function tests, thyroid function tests, vitamin B12, and autoimmune encephalitis/paraneoplastic movement-disorder antibody panel.
Surface EMG of the neck, trunk, and affected limb muscles during spontaneous posturing and attempted voluntary movement.

Surface polymyography/EMG of the neck, trunk, and bilateral upper and lower limbs during rest, passive movement, distraction, and several voluntary tasks, specifically assessing co-contraction, variability, task dependence, and incongruent muscle activation.
Prolonged video examination during gait, transfers, spontaneous activity, and distraction to document consistency and reproducibility of the dystonic postures.
Comprehensive adult-onset dystonia genetic panel, including TOR1A, THAP1, GNAL, KMT2B, ANO3, ATP1A3, GCH1, and other established dystonia genes, with deletion/duplication analysis.
served: deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses
